planting.note: Set out transplants after all frost danger has passed in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Kong is propagated from seed or cuttings and grows too large and slow from seed for most gardeners to start it themselves.

directions: Plant in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and pinch flower spikes as they appear to keep energy in the foliage. The Kong series produces some of the largest coleus leaves available, often 6–8 inches long, in bold patterns of green, burgundy, rose, and cream depending on the selection, giving a tropical, oversized-foliage effect more typical of a houseplant than a bedding annual. Its size and bold texture make it a strong focal point in large shaded containers and border plantings, though its bigger leaves need more consistent moisture and more shelter from wind than smaller-leaved coleus cultivars. Pinch growing tips periodically to encourage bushier growth, and take cuttings in late summer to overwinter indoors as houseplants.

planting.note: Set out transplants after all frost danger has passed in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; the bright chartreuse color holds best with some direct light but scorches in hot afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, and pinch flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant bushy and foliage-focused. Electric Lime is a Proven Winners coleus grown for its nearly solid, glowing chartreuse-lime leaves, one of the brightest foliage colors available for shade plantings and a strong contrast plant against dark-leaved companions like purple heuchera or bronze begonias. It tolerates more sun than many coleus cultivars without scorching, provided soil moisture stays consistent, but still performs best out of the hottest afternoon sun in Gulf South summers. Pinch tips regularly through the season to keep plants full and compact, and take cuttings before frost to overwinter indoors.

planting.note: Plant in shallow, very well-drained, peat-based, slightly acidic soil in bright indirect shade; rex begonias have shallow root systems and perform best in wide, shallow containers rather than deep pots.

directions: Plant in shallow, very well-drained, peat-based soil in bright indirect shade, keeping the soil evenly moist but never soggy, since the rhizome rots quickly in wet conditions. Escargot is one of the most recognizable rex begonia cultivars, its rounded leaves marked with a bold, concentric silver-and-green spiral radiating from a dark center in a pattern that closely resembles a snail's shell, giving the plant its name. Like other rex begonias, it is grown almost entirely for its dramatic foliage rather than its small, inconspicuous flowers, and makes an outstanding container specimen for shaded porches and patios where the spiral pattern can be appreciated up close. Divide congested rhizomes in spring, or root individual leaf cuttings in moist peat to propagate new plants.

planting.note: Plant in rich, well-drained, peat-based soil in partial to full shade; Gryphon is more sun- and drought-tolerant than most rex begonias and adapts well to both containers and shaded beds.

directions: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and allow the soil surface to dry slightly between waterings, since Gryphon tolerates drier conditions better than most rhizomatous begonias. A vigorous hybrid between rex and rhizomatous begonia types, Gryphon produces large, deeply cut, star-shaped leaves in silvery-gray overlaid with dark green veining and a near-black center, giving it a bold, almost fern-like texture unlike the smooth, rounded leaves of typical rex begonias. Its sturdier constitution and greater tolerance for brighter light and occasional dryness make it a better choice than most rex begonias for shaded outdoor beds rather than only pampered containers. Divide congested clumps in spring to propagate and rejuvenate older plantings.

planting.note: Set out transplants after frost danger passes in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; unlike smaller wax begonias, the Big series tolerates more direct sun without scorching.

directions: Plant in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, spacing plants 14–18 inches apart to fill in as a bold, season-long bedding display. Big Red is part of a landscape begonia series bred for scale, producing much larger leaves and flowers than traditional wax begonias on plants that reach 18–24 inches, with glossy bronze-green foliage and clusters of bright red flowers produced continuously from planting until frost. Its larger size and heat tolerance make it a strong mass-planting choice for beds and borders in Gulf South summer heat, where it keeps flowering with minimal deadheading required. It requires no pinching to stay full and holds up better to summer downpours than smaller, more delicate bedding begonias.

common_name: Richmondensis Begonia (Bronze-Leaf Heirloom Angel Wing Begonia)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in rich, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this old hybrid roots readily from stem cuttings and is rarely grown from seed.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings in rich, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, pinching young plants to encourage the branching, cane-like habit typical of angel wing begonias. A hybrid dating to the early 20th century still valued today, Richmondensis bears glossy, bronze-green, angel-wing-shaped leaves with a reddish underside and hanging clusters of soft pink flowers produced through summer and fall. Its tough, easy-care constitution and heirloom pedigree have kept it in circulation among begonia collectors and Southern gardeners for generations, tolerating both container culture and shaded garden beds. Take stem cuttings in late summer to overwinter indoors where winters bring hard freezes.

common_name: Mystic Spires Salvia (Compact Deep Purple Spike Salvia)

planting.note: Set out transplants after frost danger passes in well-drained soil in full sun; Mystic Spires is a sterile hybrid propagated only from cuttings, not seed.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, and deadhead or shear spent spikes periodically to keep new flowers coming through the long bloom season. Mystic Spires is a compact hybrid between mealycup sage and Salvia longispatha, producing dense, deep violet-blue flower spikes on a tidier, more floriferous plant than the taller straight species, blooming continuously from late spring to frost without going to seed and slowing down, since it sets no viable seed. Its long bloom season and steady nectar supply make it a strong performer for pollinator gardens, drawing bees and hummingbirds throughout the growing season. Perennial in zones 8–11; treat as a warm-season annual or bring potted plants indoors before frost farther north.

common_name: Electra Heuchera (Gold Foliage with Red Veins Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; the bright gold color holds best out of the hottest afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in partial shade to light shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil, providing afternoon shade protection in hot climates to keep the bright foliage color from fading. Electra is a Terra Nova Nurseries heuchera grown for its striking bright gold to chartreuse leaves overlaid with a network of contrasting deep-red veins, a color combination that stands out sharply among green- and purple-leaved shade perennials. In early summer it sends up airy, wiry stems of small white flowers above the foliage that attract hummingbirds and beneficial pollinators. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in spring, replanting divisions slightly deeper than their original position since the crown tends to lift out of the soil over time.

common_name: Black Taffeta Heuchera (Ruffled Near-Black Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; dark foliage color holds best out of intense afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in partial shade to light shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil, providing afternoon shade protection in hot climates. Black Taffeta produces large, heavily ruffled and puckered leaves in an intense near-black purple with a glossy, almost metallic sheen, one of the darkest and most texturally dramatic heuchera cultivars available, holding its deep color through the growing season better than many dark-leaved heucheras that fade to bronze in summer heat. Its bold, ruffled texture and near-black color create a striking anchor point when paired with chartreuse hostas, silver-leaved brunnera, or bright-flowered shade perennials. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in spring, replanting slightly deeper than the original position as the crown lifts over time.

common_name: Forever Red Heuchera (Season-Long Deep Red Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; deep color holds year-round with some winter chill.

directions: Plant in partial shade to light shade in well-drained, humus-rich soil, providing afternoon shade protection in hot climates to keep the deep color from bleaching out. Forever Red is a Proven Winners heuchera bred to hold its rich, deep wine-red foliage color consistently from spring through winter, unlike many red- and purple-leaved heucheras that fade to green or bronze as the season progresses. Compact and dense, it forms a tidy mound well suited to border edges, rock gardens, and mixed containers, sending up small white flowers on wiry stems in early summer that draw hummingbirds and pollinators. Divide congested clumps every 3–4 years in spring, replanting divisions slightly deeper than their original position as the crown lifts over time.
